theory.question: Distinguish schema-on-read from schema-on-write.
theory.answer:
Schema-on-write is analogous to static type checking: the database catches missing or wrongly typed fields at insert time, every row is guaranteed to have the expected columns, and queries can assume a uniform structure. Adding a new column requires a migration (ALTER TABLE + UPDATE), which on large tables can mean minutes of downtime (MySQL copies the entire table) or a carefully orchestrated online migration.

Schema-on-read is analogous to dynamic type checking: new fields can be added to new documents without touching old ones, and application code handles both shapes. This is advantageous when different objects have genuinely different structures, when the schema is determined by an external system you do not control, or when the schema is evolving rapidly and migrations are costly.

Comment: PostgreSQL JSONB gives you both: a relational table (schema-on-write) with a JSONB column inside it (schema-on-read) for flexible attributes.

theory.question: Explain why normalization uses IDs instead of duplicating human-readable strings.
theory.answer:
In practice: if you store 'Greater Seattle Area' as a plain string in 10,000 user rows and the region is renamed, you need a bulk UPDATE touching every one of those rows. If you store a region_id foreign key and keep the name in a single regions table, one UPDATE on one row propagates everywhere automatically.

Normalization naturally produces many-to-one relationships (many users → one region), which require joins at read time. Document databases handle this poorly since joins are weak or absent, forcing a choice between denormalization (with its consistency risk) or multiple round-trips in application code.

theory.question: Describe when the document model breaks down and when it is appropriate to use.
theory.answer:
Imperative vs. declarative — the core difference:
An imperative query language (e.g., a for-loop in application code, or the old MongoDB query API) tells the database or runtime exactly how to find the data: iterate through these records, check this condition, collect the matches. The sequence of steps is fixed by the programmer.
A declarative query language (SQL, CSS, Datalog) describes only what the result should look like. The system — database engine or browser — decides how to produce it: which index to use, in what order to scan, whether to parallelize.

A CSS comparison makes this concrete: CSS declaratively selects elements by pattern and applies styles; the browser handles invalidation automatically. Equivalent imperative JavaScript must manually remove styles when conditions change, and must be rewritten to use new browser APIs. SQL has the same property — adding an index does not require changing any query.

For daily work: when you write application code that iterates over rows and filters them in memory, you are writing an imperative query. That bypasses the optimizer, disables indexes, and pulls data over the network unnecessarily. If the filter can be expressed in SQL, it should be.

theory.question: Describe data locality (how data is stored physically) in document storage and when it matters.
theory.answer:
In a normalized relational schema, rendering a user profile requires joining users, positions, education, and contact tables — multiple index lookups and potentially multiple disk seeks. In a document store, the whole profile is one blob, loaded in a single read.

Locality is not unique to document databases. Google Spanner allows table rows to be interleaved within a parent table. Oracle has multi-table index cluster tables. Cassandra and HBase use column families. The principle is the same: group data that is accessed together, physically together.

Comment: Locality matters most when documents map directly to a single UI view and are loaded atomically. It matters less for analytical queries that only touch a few fields across many rows.

theory.question: You have a User object in your application code with nested lists: a list of job positions and a list of education entries. Describe what problems arise when you store and reload this object using a relational database, and how a document database handles it differently.
theory.answer:
The concrete problem: a User object in application code has a list of positions and a list of education entries. In a relational database, those become separate tables linked by foreign keys. Every read requires joining them back together; every write requires coordinated inserts across multiple tables. ORM frameworks like ActiveRecord and Hibernate reduce the boilerplate but cannot fully hide the mismatch — the N+1 query problem, eager vs. lazy loading decisions, and migration coordination all leak through.

Document databases reduce this friction for entities that are naturally tree-shaped and loaded in full. A résumé as a JSON document maps closely to the object in memory: one fetch, one object, no translation. The mismatch reappears as soon as the entity grows relationships to other entities (company pages, recommendations) that cannot be embedded.

For daily engineering, the practical implication is: evaluate your most common read pattern first. If it always loads the full entity, a document model or a JSONB column may simplify your code. If you frequently query subsets of fields across many rows, the relational model wins.

theory.question: Explain what's the difference between declarative and imperative query languages and why declarative query languages like SQL outperform imperative query APIs.
theory.answer:
A CSS comparison makes this concrete: CSS declaratively selects elements by pattern and applies styles; the browser handles invalidation automatically. Equivalent imperative JavaScript must manually remove styles when conditions change, and must be rewritten to use new browser APIs. SQL has the same property — adding an index does not require changing any query.

For daily work: when you write application code that iterates over rows and filters them in memory, you are writing an imperative query. That bypasses the optimizer, disables indexes, and pulls data over the network unnecessarily. If the filter can be expressed in SQL, it should be.

theory.question: PostgreSQL added a JSON column type; MongoDB added a SQL-like aggregation pipeline. What does this tell you about the long-term direction of relational vs. document databases, and what does it mean for picking a database for a new project?
theory.answer:
On the relational side: PostgreSQL (since 9.3), MySQL (since 5.7), and IBM DB2 (since 10.5) support JSON columns with querying and indexing inside the JSON. This lets relational databases store heterogeneous, schema-on-read data in a single column while keeping the surrounding schema strict.

On the document side: RethinkDB supports relational-like joins in its query language. Some MongoDB drivers automatically resolve database references, effectively performing a client-side join. MongoDB added the aggregation pipeline — a declarative query language that resembles SQL, showing that NoSQL systems tend to reinvent relational concepts over time.

For practical architecture decisions, convergence means you often do not need to choose between relational and document: PostgreSQL with JSONB gives you both in one system. Fully normalized tables for entities with stable structure and many-to-many relationships; JSONB columns for flexible attributes, heterogeneous event payloads, or external data whose shape you do not control. This reduces operational overhead compared to running two separate database systems.

practice.question:

practice.answer:
Return `"relational"` for inventory (tabular entities + FKs + transactions), `"graph"` for fraud (variable-depth edge traversal), and `"document"` for IoT (heterogeneous, schema-on-read payloads). Decision rule in plain prose: draw the main entities and relationships — a tree of self-contained objects points to document; flat tables with foreign keys and uniform rows point to relational; a web where you follow edges of variable depth points to graph. Most real systems mix these (for example relational core plus a JSON column for flexible attributes).

A job-board stores company name, city, and category as plain strings inside each posting row. Renaming a company therefore requires updating every duplicated string. Then normalize so a company rename updates exactly one row.

Prerequisites: PostgreSQL 16+ with `psql` on your PATH.

```sql
-- PostgreSQL
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ch2_job_postings_raw CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ch2_job_postings  CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ch2_companies     CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ch2_cities        CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ch2_job_categories CASCADE;

CREATE TABLE ch2_job_postings_raw (
  id           SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  title        TEXT NOT NULL,
  company_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  city         TEXT NOT NULL,
  category     TEXT NOT NULL
);


-- Part A stubs: denormalized rename
UPDATE ch2_job_postings_raw
SET    company_name = company_name  -- implement: set to 'Acme Technologies' where name is 'Acme Corp'
WHERE  FALSE;                       -- implement: company_name = 'Acme Corp'

SELECT id, title, company_name
FROM   ch2_job_postings_raw
WHERE  FALSE;  -- implement: company_name = 'Acme Technologies'

-- Part B stubs: normalize, then rename one lookup row
-- implement: CREATE lookup tables ch2_companies, ch2_cities, ch2_job_categories (id SERIAL PK, name TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL)
-- implement: CREATE ch2_job_postings (title + company_id/city_id/category_id FKs to the lookups)
-- implement: INSERT DISTINCT names into each lookup from ch2_job_postings_raw
-- implement: INSERT migrate postings via JOINs on company_name/city/category to lookup ids
-- implement: UPDATE ch2_companies rename 'Acme Technologies' -> 'Acme Corp Inc' (one row; raw already renamed in Part A)
-- implement: SELECT jp.title, company, city, category via JOINs WHERE company = 'Acme Corp Inc' (expect 5 rows)
```

Tasks:
1. Write the UPDATE that sets `company_name` to `'Acme Technologies'` wherever it is `'Acme Corp'`, then SELECT the renamed rows and confirm 5 postings were affected.
2. Create lookup tables `ch2_companies`, `ch2_cities`, and `ch2_job_categories` (each with `id` and unique `name`), create `ch2_job_postings` with FKs, and migrate from `ch2_job_postings_raw` (DISTINCT inserts + JOIN migration). Use the current raw names after Part A (`'Acme Technologies'`, `'Bright Systems'`, etc.).
3. Rename `'Acme Technologies'` to `'Acme Corp Inc'` with a single-row UPDATE on `ch2_companies`.
4. SELECT joining postings to lookups and verify all Acme postings show the new name (5 rows) without updating posting rows.

A notification service stores the same messages twice: once in a relational table and once as JSONB payloads. Add a priority field with a schema-on-write migration, query priority under schema-on-read without a migration, then add `ttl_seconds` only to push rows.

Prerequisites: PostgreSQL 16+ with `psql` on your PATH.

```sql
-- PostgreSQL
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ch2_notif_relational CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ch2_notif_document  CASCADE;

CREATE TABLE ch2_notif_relational (
  id         SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id    INT  NOT NULL,
  type       TEXT NOT NULL,
  message    TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE ch2_notif_document (
  id         SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id    INT  NOT NULL,
  type       TEXT NOT NULL,
  payload    JSONB NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);



-- Part A: schema-on-write — add priority with a default for every existing row
ALTER TABLE ch2_notif_relational
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS priority TEXT;  -- implement: use NOT NULL DEFAULT 'normal' instead of nullable TEXT

UPDATE ch2_notif_relational
SET    priority = priority  -- implement: set priority = 'high'
WHERE  FALSE;               -- implement: type = 'sms'

SELECT id, user_id, type, message, created_at
       -- implement: also select priority
FROM   ch2_notif_relational;

-- Part B: schema-on-read — return message and a consistent priority for every JSONB row
SELECT
  id,
  type,
  payload->>'message' AS message,
  -- implement COALESCE for missing priority (default 'normal')
  NULL AS priority
FROM ch2_notif_document;

-- Part C: patch only push rows with ttl_seconds = 86400 via JSONB || merge
UPDATE ch2_notif_document
SET    payload = payload  -- implement || merge of '{"ttl_seconds": 86400}'::jsonb
WHERE  type = 'push';

  -- implement: include "ttl_seconds": 3600 in the payload JSON above

SELECT type, payload->>'message' AS message
       -- implement: also select payload->>'ttl_seconds' AS ttl
FROM   ch2_notif_document;
```

Tasks:
1. ALTER TABLE to add `priority TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'normal'`, UPDATE SMS rows to `priority = 'high'`, and SELECT including `priority` (SMS high, others normal).
2. Write the JSONB SELECT that returns `message` and a consistent `priority` for every row — use `'normal'` when the key is absent (no schema migration).
3. UPDATE push rows so `payload` gains `ttl_seconds = 86400` using `||`, INSERT a new push with `ttl_seconds = 3600`, and SELECT `type`, message, and `ttl_seconds` for every row.
practice.answer:
Schema-on-write enforces priority on every relational row via ALTER + UPDATE. Schema-on-read leaves JSONB untouched and defaults missing keys in the query. Selective JSONB merge adds `ttl_seconds` only to push rows — email/SMS simply lack the key.

```sql
-- PostgreSQL
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ch2_notif_relational CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ch2_notif_document  CASCADE;

CREATE TABLE ch2_notif_relational (
  id         SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id    INT  NOT NULL,
  type       TEXT NOT NULL,
  message    TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE ch2_notif_document (
  id         SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id    INT  NOT NULL,
  type       TEXT NOT NULL,
  payload    JSONB NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

INSERT INTO ch2_notif_relational (user_id, type, message) VALUES
  (1, 'email', 'Your order #1042 has shipped'),
  (2, 'push',  'Flash sale: 40% off electronics'),
  (3, 'sms',   'Your verification code is 8271'),
  (1, 'push',  'Your package was delivered');

INSERT INTO ch2_notif_document (user_id, type, payload) VALUES
  (1, 'email', '{"message": "Your order #1042 has shipped",    "to": "alice@example.com", "subject": "Order update"}'),
  (2, 'push',  '{"message": "Flash sale: 40% off electronics",  "device_token": "tok_abc", "badge": 1}'),
  (3, 'sms',   '{"message": "Your verification code is 8271",   "phone": "+49123456789", "priority": "high"}'),
  (1, 'push',  '{"message": "Your package was delivered",        "device_token": "tok_abc", "badge": 2}');

-- Part A: schema-on-write
ALTER TABLE ch2_notif_relational
  ADD COLUMN priority TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'normal';

UPDATE ch2_notif_relational
SET    priority = 'high'
WHERE  type = 'sms';

SELECT id, user_id, type, message, priority, created_at
FROM   ch2_notif_relational;
-- sms: high; email/push: normal

-- Part B: schema-on-read
SELECT
  id,
  type,
  payload->>'message' AS message,
  COALESCE(payload->>'priority', 'normal') AS priority
FROM ch2_notif_document;
-- old email/push: normal via COALESCE; sms: high from payload

-- Part C: selective JSONB patch
UPDATE ch2_notif_document
SET    payload = payload || '{"ttl_seconds": 86400}'::jsonb
WHERE  type = 'push';

INSERT INTO ch2_notif_document (user_id, type, payload) VALUES
  (2, 'push', '{"message": "New message from Sarah",
               "device_token": "tok_xyz", "badge": 3, "ttl_seconds": 3600}');

SELECT type, payload->>'message' AS message, payload->>'ttl_seconds' AS ttl
FROM   ch2_notif_document;
-- email/sms: ttl NULL (key absent); push: 86400 or 3600
```

The relational equivalent of Part C would be `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ttl_seconds INT` plus an UPDATE — every email/SMS row would carry a confusing NULL. Schema-on-read avoids that but requires every query to handle missing keys (forgotten COALESCE hides bugs as silent NULLs).

An online store records orders with category, city, amount, and timestamp. Compute revenue aggregates declaratively in SQL, then simulate the MapReduce map/reduce approach with CTEs for the same monthly category revenue.

Prerequisites: PostgreSQL 16+ with `psql` on your PATH.

```sql
-- PostgreSQL
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ch2_orders CASCADE;

CREATE TABLE ch2_orders (
  id          SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT           NOT NULL,
  category    TEXT          NOT NULL,
  city        TEXT          NOT NULL,
  amount      NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,
  placed_at   TIMESTAMP     NOT NULL
);


-- Part A: monthly category revenue
SELECT
  -- implement date_trunc month + category GROUP BY and SUM(amount)
  NULL AS month,
  NULL AS category,
  NULL AS revenue
FROM ch2_orders;

-- Part A: top category per city via window
WITH city_cat AS (
  -- implement GROUP BY city, category with SUM(amount) AS revenue
  SELECT NULL AS city, NULL AS category, NULL AS revenue
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT city, category, revenue,
         -- implement RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY revenue DESC)
         NULL AS rnk
  FROM city_cat
)
SELECT city, category, revenue FROM ranked WHERE rnk = 1 ORDER BY city;

-- Part B: MapReduce-style CTEs (map then reduce)
WITH
  mapped AS (
    SELECT
      -- implement map-key: YYYY-MM|category composite key
      NULL AS key,
      amount AS value
    FROM ch2_orders
  ),
  reduced AS (
    SELECT key,
           -- implement reduce-SUM of value GROUP BY key
           NULL AS revenue
    FROM   mapped
    GROUP BY key
  )
SELECT split_part(key,'|',1) AS month, split_part(key,'|',2) AS category, revenue
FROM   reduced
ORDER BY month, revenue DESC;

-- Part B: same pipeline with a post-aggregation filter (revenue > 200)
WITH mapped AS (
    SELECT
      -- implement map-key (same as above)
      NULL AS key,
      amount AS value
    FROM ch2_orders
),
reduced AS (
    SELECT key,
           -- implement reduce-SUM
           NULL AS revenue
    FROM mapped
    GROUP BY key
)
SELECT split_part(key,'|',1) AS month, split_part(key,'|',2) AS category, revenue
FROM   reduced
WHERE  TRUE  -- implement post-aggregation filter: revenue > 200
ORDER BY month, revenue DESC;
```

```sql
  (9, 'Clothing',    'Berlin',     69.99, '2024-03-08 15:00:00'),
  (10,'Books',       'Amsterdam',  24.99, '2024-03-15 09:00:00');

-- Revenue per category per month
SELECT
  to_char(date_trunc('month', placed_at), 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
  category,
  SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM   ch2_orders
GROUP BY date_trunc('month', placed_at), category
ORDER BY month, revenue DESC;

-- Top category per city (window function — would need a second MapReduce job)
WITH city_cat AS (
  SELECT city, category, SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM   ch2_orders
  GROUP BY city, category
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT city, category, revenue,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rnk
  FROM city_cat
)
SELECT city, category, revenue FROM ranked WHERE rnk = 1 ORDER BY city;

-- MapReduce-style CTEs
WITH
  mapped AS (
    SELECT
      to_char(date_trunc('month', placed_at), 'YYYY-MM') || '|' || category AS key,
      amount AS value
    FROM ch2_orders
  ),
  reduced AS (
    SELECT key, SUM(value) AS revenue
    FROM   mapped
    GROUP BY key
  )
SELECT split_part(key,'|',1) AS month, split_part(key,'|',2) AS category, revenue
FROM   reduced
ORDER BY month, revenue DESC;

-- Post-aggregation filter (HAVING in SQL; extra stage in MapReduce)
WITH mapped AS (
    SELECT to_char(date_trunc('month',placed_at),'YYYY-MM')||'|'||category AS key,
           amount AS value FROM ch2_orders
),
reduced AS (SELECT key, SUM(value) AS revenue FROM mapped GROUP BY key)
SELECT split_part(key,'|',1) AS month, split_part(key,'|',2) AS category, revenue
FROM   reduced WHERE revenue > 200 ORDER BY month, revenue DESC;
```

The optimizer chooses indexes, join order, and whether to parallelize. Plain GROUP BY is preferred for day-to-day SQL; the CTE form is useful for seeing what MapReduce does: map emits (key, value) pairs, reduce sums all pairs with the same key.

A package registry stores packages and their declared dependencies as a directed graph. Resolve myapp's direct and transitive dependencies, then find every package broken by a change to utils.

Prerequisites: PostgreSQL 16+ with `psql` on your PATH.

```sql
-- PostgreSQL
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ch2_deps     CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ch2_packages CASCADE;

CREATE TABLE ch2_packages (
  id      INT  PRIMARY KEY,
  name    TEXT NOT NULL,
  version TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE ch2_deps (
  package_id    INT REFERENCES ch2_packages(id),
  depends_on_id INT REFERENCES ch2_packages(id),
  PRIMARY KEY (package_id, depends_on_id)
);


-- myapp -> webserver -> router -> http-lib
--                    -> logger  -> utils
-- myapp -> logger
-- router -> crypto

-- Part B stub: recursive CTE for all transitive deps of myapp with min hop count
WITH RECURSIVE all_deps AS (
  -- implement: base case — direct deps of myapp at depth 1
  SELECT NULL::int AS dep_id, NULL::int AS depth
  WHERE FALSE

  UNION  -- implement: use UNION (not UNION ALL) to avoid infinite loops if cycles exist

  -- implement: recursive step — walk outbound depends_on edges, depth + 1
  SELECT NULL::int, NULL::int
  WHERE FALSE
)
SELECT p.name, p.version, MIN(all_deps.depth) AS min_hops
FROM   all_deps
JOIN   ch2_packages p ON p.id = all_deps.dep_id
GROUP BY p.name, p.version
ORDER BY min_hops, p.name;

-- Part C stub: reverse recursive CTE — packages that depend on utils
WITH RECURSIVE dependents AS (
  -- implement: base case — packages that directly depend on utils at depth 1
  SELECT NULL::int AS pkg_id, NULL::int AS depth
  WHERE FALSE

  UNION  -- implement: use UNION (not UNION ALL) to avoid cycles

  -- implement: recursive step — follow incoming edges upward
  SELECT NULL::int, NULL::int
  WHERE FALSE
)
SELECT p.name, p.version, MIN(dependents.depth) AS hops_from_utils
FROM   dependents
JOIN   ch2_packages p ON p.id = dependents.pkg_id
GROUP BY p.name, p.version
ORDER BY hops_from_utils, p.name;
```

Expected signals: direct deps of myapp are `webserver` and `logger`; transitive hops — hop 1 `logger`/`webserver`, hop 2 `router`/`utils`, hop 3 `crypto`/`http-lib`; reverse dependents of `utils` are `logger`, `webserver`, and `myapp`.

Tasks:
1. Implement the SELECT so it returns the packages `myapp` directly depends on (no recursion): `webserver` and `logger`.
2. Implement the recursive CTE so it walks every reachable dependency of `myapp` and returns each package with its minimum hop count. Use `UNION` (not `UNION ALL`). Confirm hop 1 `logger`/`webserver`, hop 2 `router`/`utils`, hop 3 `crypto`/`http-lib`.
3. Implement the reverse recursive CTE that starts from `utils` and follows incoming edges upward. Confirm affected packages are `logger`, `webserver`, and `myapp`.
practice.answer:
Full seed plus direct JOIN, forward recursive CTE, and reverse recursive CTE. Direct query returns only depth-1 deps; transitive walk is what a package manager needs; reverse walk is impact analysis before a breaking publish.

```sql
-- PostgreSQL
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ch2_deps     CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ch2_packages CASCADE;

CREATE TABLE ch2_packages (
  id      INT  PRIMARY KEY,
  name    TEXT NOT NULL,
  version TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE ch2_deps (
  package_id    INT REFERENCES ch2_packages(id),
  depends_on_id INT REFERENCES ch2_packages(id),
  PRIMARY KEY (package_id, depends_on_id)
);

INSERT INTO ch2_packages VALUES
  (1,'myapp','1.0.0'),(2,'webserver','2.3.1'),(3,'router','1.4.0'),
  (4,'http-lib','3.1.0'),(5,'logger','2.0.0'),(6,'utils','1.1.0'),(7,'crypto','4.2.0');

INSERT INTO ch2_deps VALUES (1,2),(1,5),(2,3),(2,5),(3,4),(3,7),(5,6);

-- Part A: direct dependencies of myapp
SELECT p.name AS dependency, p.version
FROM   ch2_deps d
JOIN   ch2_packages p ON p.id = d.depends_on_id
WHERE  d.package_id = (SELECT id FROM ch2_packages WHERE name = 'myapp');
-- Returns: webserver, logger

-- Part B: all transitive deps with min hop count
WITH RECURSIVE all_deps AS (
  SELECT d.depends_on_id AS dep_id, 1 AS depth
  FROM   ch2_deps d
  JOIN   ch2_packages root ON root.id = d.package_id AND root.name = 'myapp'

  UNION

  SELECT d.depends_on_id, ad.depth + 1
  FROM   ch2_deps d
  JOIN   all_deps ad ON ad.dep_id = d.package_id
)
SELECT p.name, p.version, MIN(all_deps.depth) AS min_hops
FROM   all_deps
JOIN   ch2_packages p ON p.id = all_deps.dep_id
GROUP BY p.name, p.version
ORDER BY min_hops, p.name;
-- hop 1: logger, webserver
-- hop 2: router (via webserver), utils (via logger)
-- hop 3: crypto, http-lib (via router)

-- Part C: reverse walk from utils
WITH RECURSIVE dependents AS (
  SELECT d.package_id AS pkg_id, 1 AS depth
  FROM   ch2_deps d
  JOIN   ch2_packages u ON u.id = d.depends_on_id AND u.name = 'utils'

  UNION

  SELECT d.package_id, dep.depth + 1
  FROM   ch2_deps d
  JOIN   dependents dep ON dep.pkg_id = d.depends_on_id
)
SELECT p.name, p.version, MIN(dependents.depth) AS hops_from_utils
FROM   dependents
JOIN   ch2_packages p ON p.id = dependents.pkg_id
GROUP BY p.name, p.version
ORDER BY hops_from_utils, p.name;
-- Affected: logger (direct), webserver (via logger), myapp (via both paths)
```

UNION deduplicates packages reachable via multiple paths. Equivalent Cypher for the forward walk is roughly one MATCH with a variable-length path; SQL can express the same pattern but with more syntax. Graph databases make reverse traversal equally natural as forward traversal — here it is the same recursive CTE with the JOIN direction flipped.

```sql
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ch2_products CASCADE;

  type  TEXT           NOT NULL,

  attrs JSONB          NOT NULL

       NULL AS ram_gb,          -- implement: (attrs->>'ram_gb')::int

-- Part B: insert out-of-stock book 'Refactoring' with in_stock:false in attrs
  -- implement: attrs with book fields + in_stock:false (see Tasks)
```

```sql
  ('Clean Code',                'book',          35.99, '{"author":"Robert C. Martin","pages":431,"isbn":"978-0-13-235088-4","year":2008}'),
  ('The Pragmatic Programmer',  'book',          49.99, '{"author":"David Thomas",     "pages":352,"isbn":"978-0-13-595705-9","year":2019}');

-- Part A
SELECT name, (attrs->>'ram_gb')::int AS ram_gb,
             (attrs->>'display_inch')::float AS display_inch
FROM   ch2_products
WHERE  type = 'electronics'
  AND  (attrs->>'ram_gb')::int >= 16;
-- ThinkPad X1 Carbon (16 GB), Dell XPS 15 (32 GB)

SELECT name, price, attrs->'colors' AS colors
FROM   ch2_products
WHERE  type = 'clothing'
  AND  attrs->'sizes' ? 'M';
-- Merino Wool Sweater, Waterproof Running Jacket

-- Part B
UPDATE ch2_products
SET    attrs = attrs || '{"in_stock": true}'::jsonb;

INSERT INTO ch2_products (name, type, price, attrs) VALUES
  ('Refactoring', 'book', 44.99,
   '{"author": "Martin Fowler", "pages": 448,
     "isbn": "978-0-13-468599-1", "year": 2018, "in_stock": false}');

SELECT name, type, attrs->>'in_stock' AS in_stock FROM ch2_products ORDER BY name;

-- Part C
INSERT INTO ch2_products (name, type, price, attrs)
VALUES ('Mystery Gadget', 'electronics', 59.00, '{"ram_gb": 4}');

SELECT name, attrs->>'cpu' AS cpu, attrs->>'ram_gb' AS ram
FROM   ch2_products WHERE type = 'electronics';
-- Mystery Gadget: cpu = NULL — silent, discovered only at query time.

CREATE TABLE electronics (
  id           SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name         TEXT          NOT NULL,
  price        NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,
  cpu          TEXT          NOT NULL,
  ram_gb       INT           NOT NULL,
  storage_gb   INT           NOT NULL,
  display_inch NUMERIC(4,1)
);

INSERT INTO electronics (name, price, ram_gb, storage_gb)
VALUES ('Mystery Gadget', 59.00, 4, 0);
-- ERROR: null value in column "cpu" violates not-null constraint
```

The `::int` cast is required because `->>` returns text. `||` merges keys without ALTER TABLE but still rewrites row versions under MVCC. Schema-on-read's weakness: missing required fields are not caught at write time and surface as silent NULLs far from the insert site.

A blog platform indexes articles as JSON documents in Elasticsearch. Each document has a free-text `body` field, a `tags` array, and a numeric `views` field. Run relevance-ranked search, a numeric+text filter, and a per-author aggregation.

Prerequisites: Elasticsearch 8+ reachable at `http://localhost:9200`, plus DBeaver with the Elasticsearch driver for the SQL queries.

```sql
-- Part A: full-text search ranked by BM25 relevance for body matching 'caching scaling'
SELECT title, author, views, SCORE() AS relevance
FROM   "ch2_articles"
WHERE  FALSE  -- implement: MATCH(body, 'caching scaling')
ORDER BY relevance DESC;

-- Part A: articles with views > 800 whose body matches 'database', ordered by views DESC
SELECT title, author, views
FROM   "ch2_articles"
WHERE  FALSE  -- implement: MATCH(body, 'database') AND views > 800
ORDER BY views DESC;

-- Part B: COUNT articles and SUM views per author, filtered to tag sql
SELECT author, COUNT(*) AS articles, SUM(views) AS total_views
FROM   "ch2_articles"
WHERE  FALSE  -- implement: tags = 'sql'
GROUP BY author
ORDER BY total_views DESC;
```

Tasks:

2. Complete the second query so it returns articles with more than 800 views whose body contains `'database'`, ordered by views descending.
